story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I wanted to share with you a chess analysis tool that I was building for the past week.

First of all I want to explain what is the problem that I'm trying to solve: Chess Engines such as stockfish are superior for us humans, but it's not self explanatory. A player can review their game by stockfish and it will tell them that some moves are very bad and losing, but why? This is the problem that we are trying to solve.

ChessRabbit acts as a chess agent with stockfish evaluation tools. It takes every move that the player plays and it reasons about it, with the help, validation, and confirmation of Stockfish.

So instead of showing the user: "Blunder", we show them: "This is a blunder because your opponent plays Rook to d6, attacking your queen and leaving your bishop on d5 overloaded and lost. You should have played Qd4 to protect your bishop in the center and maintain your coordination."

Give it a try and let me know if you have a feedback!

title.value: Show HN: ChessRabbit – The AI Chess Analysis Platform

story_text.value:
Hi HN — I’m William, a frontend engineer from Brazil, and for the past few months I’ve been building Asking.

Asking brings customer conversations from different channels into one place. It is intended for small teams that need a proper support workflow but don’t want the cost and complexity that usually come with larger platforms.

To be transparent, Asking is built on top of Chatwoot. I’m not trying to present its messaging infrastructure as something I created from scratch. I’m using it as a foundation and building a more opinionated product around it, with simpler onboarding, inbox configuration, subscriptions, email setup, and a less overwhelming experience overall.

The project started with a question: how much customer support software does a small business actually need?

Many products are initially simple, but become expensive as the team grows. Others provide every feature imaginable, but require small companies to adopt workflows and concepts they may never need.

With Asking, I’m trying to find a better balance: enough structure to manage customer support properly, without turning it into an enterprise system.

One question I’m still exploring is whether small teams genuinely want fewer features, or whether they want the same capabilities with much less friction.

The product is still early, and I’d genuinely appreciate direct feedback — especially about what Asking would need before you could consider replacing your current support tool with it.

title.value: Show HN: Asking – A simpler customer support inbox for small teams

story_text.value:
Hi HN, Yura here, co-founder of Alphie.

In my previous YC company, we got a lot of good traffic, but only about 3% of it ever converted to demos.

We tried RB2B and many other visitor resolution tools - but weren't happy with the accuracy.

So, after that company was acquired, we decided to build our own platform.

We've found a way to achieve a much higher ID rate and accuracy than most of the previous-generation visitor ID tools.

Company-level visitor identification is about 3 times more accurate than individual-level. We use a waterfall of several data providers to boost it a bit further. Then an agent analyzes your ICP, figures out the decision-makers - and closes the loop by enriching their data. The thing is, for B2B, knowing who was the actual person that visited your website matters less than knowing that a certain company is in the market.

An unexpected side effect is that about 30% of companies can be identified via reverse IP lookup, which takes less than a second.

This allows you to do two key things for conversion:

Display content uniquely tailored to this visitor (e.g. a fintech startup sees a case study for a Series B payment platform). Rank them against your ICP - so you know if an important buyer is currently browsing your pricing page.

Alphie does the personalization in the chatbot only so far, personalizing answers and showing relevant bits of content, but potentially it could be possible to generate a whole personalized version of the landing page.

The ICP ranking is super interesting, because it allows you to pull in a human rep while the buyer is still on the website - the moment of highest intent.

We're currently running 16 pilots, 10 of them with YC companies.

Would love to hear your thoughts. Happy to answer anything, especially on the identification accuracy tradeoffs and the privacy architecture. Video Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFjQwGfsR0k Interactive demo: https://meetalphie.com/demo/app.html

title.value: Show HN: Alphie – see who's on your website and chat with them from Slack

story_text.value:
Taste Library is a web app that lets you manage and show off your collection. It's like Delicious Library, but for the web.

Here is the link: https://tastelibrary.app

I missed Delicious Library enough that I wrote about trying to recreate it last year (which was also on HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42860141). I love its design, and miss the “Delicious Generation” movement that embraced pixel-perfect, personal and fun designs. I wanted Taste Library to carry some of that spirit. I don’t want it to feel like another generic database app. I want it to feel visual, playful, and enjoyable to browse.

Taste Library is currently a UI prototype. There's no backend yet, but the demo library is nearly fully interactive. You can add things, search, reorder what you have, and manage shelves. All pages work on both desktop and mobile. I'm deliberately working out the interaction and visual design first, and I'd especially like feedback on that before building the rest.

Please give it a try at https://tastelibrary.app and let me know what you think in the comments.

title.value: Show HN: Taste Library, a Spiritual Successor to Delicious Library

We post trained a cyber-security small llm, changed how it reasons and supplemented our controls using program analysis techniques such as inline reference monitoring to outperform GPT5.5-xhigh on hard benchmarks like LinuxArena and SleightBench.

Free product available at harden.run and full benchmarks in the blog post.

story_text.value:
I love Balatro and have had a fascination with daily games recently. RNGdle in particular sparked my interest because of its dopamine-factory style gameplay. Per Diem takes a similar approach.

In Per Diem, each day you cast 5 dice from a sack randomly. The pips and patterns (ie. snake eyes) are scored, producing your final score for the day. You get one roll a day, so the challenge is maximizing your scoring potential. Charms are the mechanism by which you tilt the odds in your favour: charms can modify the pip score and the multiplier. Each day presents a new "encounter" which slightly modifies the rules of the game, requiring a new strategic approach.

Because charms are not freely available, the game scales over days as you score points, earn coins, and purchase better charms from the shop. In order to keep your score and charms you should sign in. Currently only Discord sign ins are supported - this is admittedly a bit of a growth hack: when you sign in, you can see a leaderboard for each Discord server you're apart of, which makes competition a little more fun.

I made this mostly as a fun way to test out my knowledge on how to build a viral product with some built in growth mechanisms, and now I'm testing to see if it holds up against an audience like HN. :) Let me know what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Per Diem, a daily dice game like Balatro
